## What drives the price of eggs
Retail egg prices are unusually volatile because supply can fall sharply and suddenly. Most U.S. eggs come from large flocks of laying hens, and outbreaks of highly pathogenic avian influenza (bird flu) force entire flocks to be culled, removing millions of layers within weeks. Rebuilding a flock to laying age takes months, so a single outbreak can keep prices elevated long after it is contained. Between shocks, the cost of feed grain — corn and soybean meal — is the main influence on what a dozen eggs costs.

Here's the shape I'd build, and it comes down to one hub, one shared home, and per-person accounts rather than shared logins.

The backbone is a single Bridge for the whole apartment, with one Hue account as the administrator. Don't run a separate Bridge or separate account per roommate. Philips Hue now lets one account hold multiple Bridges inside one Home, but automations, scenes and accessories can't cross Bridges, so splitting them only creates friction. One Bridge handles up to 50 lights and 12 accessories, with a hard ceiling of 63; the Bridge Pro goes to 150 lights and 50 accessories for around $150 versus roughly $80. A studio apartment almost certainly fits comfortably on the standard Bridge, so there's no reason to buy the Pro unless you're approaching that 50-light mark or you specifically want MotionAware, which only runs on the Pro.

For people, the trick is that each person gets their own Hue account, and you invite them into your Home as a member rather than giving them your login. In the Hue app that's Settings, Manage members, then the plus icon; they accept the email invitation while signed in as themselves. Philips offers four permission tiers, and the lowest one still includes controlling the lights, which is what you want for roommates: keep admin to yourself so nobody accidentally deletes a bulb, renames rooms or rewrites automations. If someone moves out, you remove them from the Home instead of changing a shared password. One caveat worth knowing: if a roommate's phone was ever paired directly to the Bridge without an account, that app only sees one Bridge and you lose visibility over what it does, so it's cleaner to migrate everyone onto proper accounts.

For voice, pick a single assistant ecosystem and stick with it. Running Alexa and Google Home and Apple Home against the same bulbs all at once gives you duplicate device lists and commands that only reach some of the lights. In the Hue app, go to Settings, then Smart Home, and pair through Matter, which hands you a pairing code you enter in the assistant's app. Then use that platform's own household sharing, since that's what makes multiple people's voices work: Apple Home with each person added as a family member on their own Apple ID, Google Home's home group with family managers, or Amazon Household for Alexa. Anyone in the apartment can then talk to a smart speaker or their own phone, and their automations and preferences stay theirs.

Now the internet question, which is the good news. The bulbs talk to the Bridge over Zigbee, and the Bridge talks to your router over Ethernet, so the lighting path is local and the internet is only one branch off it. If your internet drops but power and the home network are fine, the lights keep working: the Hue app on your phone over Wi-Fi still controls them, and schedules and automations stored on the Bridge keep running. Philips is explicit that whatever permission level a user has, they can always control the lights, even when the internet is down. What does stop is remote control from outside the apartment, firmware and app update behavior, account-linked extras like Spotify sync, and notifications.

Voice is the fragile part, so plan around it. Alexa and Google Assistant route requests through their own cloud, so when the internet is down they commonly fail or report a light as unresponsive even though the bulb is fine. Two ways to harden that. The stronger software option is Apple Home, which is local-first: with a HomePod or Apple TV acting as a hub, Siri commands can still be handled on your network, though results vary by setup. The genuinely bulletproof option is hardware, and I'd budget for it regardless of which assistant you pick: Hue Dimmer switches or smart buttons paired straight to the Bridge. Those work over Zigbee alone, and people in a shared apartment will thank you for them anyway, because the person whose phone battery is dead can still turn the lights off.

Two footnotes. Since September 2025 all new Hue bulbs and strips also support Matter over Thread, so a new bulb can join Apple Home or Home Assistant through a Thread border router with no Bridge at all; gradient lights are the exception and still need the Bridge. And if you want voice control that survives any outage, Home Assistant is the serious answer, since its Hue integration uses the Bridge's local push API and keeps running fully offline. I'd call that an enthusiast path, not a requirement for a studio, but it's the reason some people with Hue never touch Alexa or Google.

# How to set up multiple Bridges and Homes in a Hue account
Previously, you had to create individual Hue accounts for each Bridge you want to control. As the Hue ecosystem continually evolves to become more user-friendly and organized, you can now combine your Bridges into a single account.
So, what does this mean for you? Let’s begin with some straightforward — yet crucial — questions:
What’s a Hue account?
A Hue account is linked to your Philips Hue system, and lets you control your lights remotely, as well as manage access to your system for users and applications. For more information about accounts, please visit: https://www.philips-hue.com/account
What’s a Hue home?
A Hue Home is the representation of your physical home in the cloud. If you’re an administrator of your Home, you can manage other accounts, control their permissions, and more. With the Multi-Bridge feature, a home can support multiple Bridges alongside the already supported multiple Cameras.
What’s the Hue Bridge?
A Hue Bridge is the smart lighting hub. The Bridge makes it possible to control your lights any way you want — from anywhere with an internet connection. It provides Automations to schedule your lights to turn on and off. The Lights connected to the Bridge can be controlled by sensors, switches, and more and allows customization to your accessories. For more information about the Bridge, please visit: https://www.philips-hue.com/bridge
Why combine accounts?
It’s all in the name of streamlining your smart home. By combining them, you can:
- Simply use one email address or social login to control your lights remotely, as well as manage access to your system for users and applications for multiple Homes, Bridges and Camera’s.
- Control lights on multiple Bridges in the same Home from your Hue app’s Home tab.
- Control lights and security systems in two homes (e.g. a primary home and vacation home) with one account.
- Manage access to all your Bridges in one Home
How to set it up
Make sure you have the latest update of your Hue app, depending on the type of setup you have and what you want to do, you need to follow the step-by-step instructions below:
You have multiple Bridges linked to separate accounts and want to move one or more of the Bridges into a single Home:
Before you start, choose which Home you want to move your Bridge(s) into. We’ll call this Home A.
- In Settings, tap My Homes
a. Make sure that you have selected the right home.
b. Go back to settings
.2. In Settings, tap Bridges
- In Bridges, tap ‘+’ in upper right corner
Follow the respective steps to link the bridge.
- (Optional) In Settings, tap “Manage members” and review permissions.
- (Optional) In Settings, tap “My Homes” Remove the empty other Home.
Do you have more Bridges you want to move to Home A? Repeat this process.
Do you have bridges that are not linked to a home? And you would like to have it linked to a home and controlled more securely by somebody that also has an account? Then you can also follow this process.
You have multiple Bridges in another physical location, such as an office building or vacation house:
You can choose to keep your current setup with separate accounts, or you can move the secondary home into your primary Hue account, so that each Bridge has its own Home.
.
You have a Bridge that isn’t linked to a Home:
You have multiple bridges of which one bridge – called bridge A – is linked to a home (to which one account is associated) and one bridge – let’s call this bridge B – is directly controlled by another Hue App without an account. For some reason, you don’t want to create an account on this Hue App yet, you do want this second bridge B to be linked to your home. This allows you to still control this second Bridge B. The other Hue App can continue to use this bridge B as well – even without an account.
You can follow the steps as above.
The user of the second Hue App (right one in the picture above) can always only control one bridge. To control multiple bridges, an account must be created. Further, the user of the first Hue app – who has an account – will have less visibility and control over what the user of the second Hue App is doing. To have stronger security and ensure better privacy, it would be strongly recommended to create an account.
Using multiple Bridges and Homes
When you combine multiple Bridges in a Home — or across multiple Homes — some things change, and most things stay the same. All to make your system easier to control!
Subscriptions
It's not currently possible to move a Bridge that has a subscription linked to it (e.g., a Secure plan or Sync TV app subscription). If you have a subscription, we recommend making the account it's linked to your primary account and moving your other Bridges into it.
If you have multiple Bridges with multiple subscriptions linked to them, you won't be able to move your Bridges and keep your subscriptions at this time.
Automations, accessories, and Entertainment areas function the same as they always have. In other words, they can't control lights on different Bridges. The app shows a Bridge selector for each of these features.
Security cameras can, on the other hand, can work across multiple Bridges, so you can monitor the cameras from multiple Homes in the same account. Alarms can also be configured to work across cameras and lights from multiple Bridges linked to the same Home.
Using voice assistants
You can control your lights using voice assistant on multiple bridges.
Will all Bridges from multiple Homes — e.g., a primary residence and vacation home— also be displayed in a consolidated view in the app?
No, the app can only display and control one Home at the time. The app allows you to easily switch between Home. Only the Rooms and Zones on the Bridges in the same Home under a single account will be displayed in the Home tab.
Have more than one Home? Easily switch between them by tapping the home icon at the top of the Home tab, selecting your Home in settings->My Homes, tapping and holding the Home tab’s icon or even by tapping and holding the Hue app’s icon on your phone/tablet home screen.

exchanges.final_answer:
Here's the shape I'd build, and it comes down to one hub, one shared home, and per-person accounts rather than shared logins.

The backbone is a single Bridge for the whole apartment, with one Hue account as the administrator. Don't run a separate Bridge or separate account per roommate. Philips Hue now lets one account hold multiple Bridges inside one Home, but automations, scenes and accessories can't cross Bridges, so splitting them only creates friction. One Bridge handles up to 50 lights and 12 accessories, with a hard ceiling of 63; the Bridge Pro goes to 150 lights and 50 accessories for around $150 versus roughly $80. A studio apartment almost certainly fits comfortably on the standard Bridge, so there's no reason to buy the Pro unless you're approaching that 50-light mark or you specifically want MotionAware, which only runs on the Pro.

For people, the trick is that each person gets their own Hue account, and you invite them into your Home as a member rather than giving them your login. In the Hue app that's Settings, Manage members, then the plus icon; they accept the email invitation while signed in as themselves. Philips offers four permission tiers, and the lowest one still includes controlling the lights, which is what you want for roommates: keep admin to yourself so nobody accidentally deletes a bulb, renames rooms or rewrites automations. If someone moves out, you remove them from the Home instead of changing a shared password. One caveat worth knowing: if a roommate's phone was ever paired directly to the Bridge without an account, that app only sees one Bridge and you lose visibility over what it does, so it's cleaner to migrate everyone onto proper accounts.

For voice, pick a single assistant ecosystem and stick with it. Running Alexa and Google Home and Apple Home against the same bulbs all at once gives you duplicate device lists and commands that only reach some of the lights. In the Hue app, go to Settings, then Smart Home, and pair through Matter, which hands you a pairing code you enter in the assistant's app. Then use that platform's own household sharing, since that's what makes multiple people's voices work: Apple Home with each person added as a family member on their own Apple ID, Google Home's home group with family managers, or Amazon Household for Alexa. Anyone in the apartment can then talk to a smart speaker or their own phone, and their automations and preferences stay theirs.

Now the internet question, which is the good news. The bulbs talk to the Bridge over Zigbee, and the Bridge talks to your router over Ethernet, so the lighting path is local and the internet is only one branch off it. If your internet drops but power and the home network are fine, the lights keep working: the Hue app on your phone over Wi-Fi still controls them, and schedules and automations stored on the Bridge keep running. Philips is explicit that whatever permission level a user has, they can always control the lights, even when the internet is down. What does stop is remote control from outside the apartment, firmware and app update behavior, account-linked extras like Spotify sync, and notifications.

Voice is the fragile part, so plan around it. Alexa and Google Assistant route requests through their own cloud, so when the internet is down they commonly fail or report a light as unresponsive even though the bulb is fine. Two ways to harden that. The stronger software option is Apple Home, which is local-first: with a HomePod or Apple TV acting as a hub, Siri commands can still be handled on your network, though results vary by setup. The genuinely bulletproof option is hardware, and I'd budget for it regardless of which assistant you pick: Hue Dimmer switches or smart buttons paired straight to the Bridge. Those work over Zigbee alone, and people in a shared apartment will thank you for them anyway, because the person whose phone battery is dead can still turn the lights off.

Two footnotes. Since September 2025 all new Hue bulbs and strips also support Matter over Thread, so a new bulb can join Apple Home or Home Assistant through a Thread border router with no Bridge at all; gradient lights are the exception and still need the Bridge. And if you want voice control that survives any outage, Home Assistant is the serious answer, since its Hue integration uses the Bridge's local push API and keeps running fully offline. I'd call that an enthusiast path, not a requirement for a studio, but it's the reason some people with Hue never touch Alexa or Google.

Two separate problems, and both have pretty well understood causes. Let me take them in turn.

The choppy audio is almost certainly a radio problem. Bluetooth lives in the 2.4 gigahertz band, and so does most Wi-Fi, so when your laptop is pulling real traffic over 2.4 gigahertz while simultaneously streaming audio to the JBL, the two are sharing one crowded lane. Bluetooth tries to dodge Wi-Fi with adaptive frequency hopping, jumping among its channels hundreds of times a second, but when a Wi-Fi channel is wide or the band is congested, it runs out of clean slots and packets get dropped, which is exactly the stutter you hear. This is worse on laptops because the Wi-Fi and Bluetooth radios are usually on the same little chip and share an antenna, so they have to negotiate for airtime internally. That is why the symptom appears "when I connect my laptop" but not when something else is the source.

The other candidates worth knowing: unshielded USB 3.0 devices radiate broadband noise right into the 2.4 to 2.5 gigahertz range, so a plugged-in external drive, dock, or HDMI-to-USB adapter can act like a local jammer. Windows power management can briefly power down the Bluetooth adapter to save energy. And if the audio codec is a high-bitrate one, or the laptop is under heavy CPU load while gaming, the audio buffer can underrun and sound choppy even with a clean radio link.

Here is how I would narrow it down, one variable at a time. First, switch the laptop to a 5 or 6 gigahertz Wi-Fi network and test the same local audio. If the stutter vanishes on 5 gigahertz and returns on 2.4, you have your answer, and the fix is to keep the laptop off 2.4 gigahertz, or at least move the router to a channel farther from the edges of the band. Verify the live connection rather than assuming; on Windows, netsh wlan show interfaces tells you the band and channel you are actually on, and a laptop that supports 5 gigahertz will still quietly connect to 2.4. Second, if it stutters on every band, unplug any USB 3.0 drive, hub, or dock and see whether it clears; if it does, move that device to a USB 2.0 port or put a short shielded extension cable between it and the laptop. Third, in Device Manager, open the Bluetooth adapter's properties and turn off "allow the computer to turn off this device to save power." Fourth, update the Wi-Fi and Bluetooth drivers from the laptop manufacturer, since coexistence handling is driver-dependent and generic tweaks you read online may not exist for your chipset. Fifth, move the JBL closer to the laptop with a clear line of sight, keep it off a metal desk surface, and make sure the projector isn't also holding a Bluetooth connection or a second audio profile, since each extra link eats bandwidth. If the projector is receiving the laptop's video wirelessly over Miracast, AirPlay or a casting dongle, that is another heavy 2.4 gigahertz consumer, and switching it to 5 gigahertz or using a plain HDMI cable instead is often the single biggest improvement.

Now the eye strain, which is a different kind of problem and also fairly predictable. The biggest factor is refresh rate and motion handling. A typical projector runs at 60 hertz, while a gaming monitor is often 120 to 144 hertz or more, so fast motion on the projector has more strobing and blur, and your eyes keep trying to track targets that the display isn't actually rendering smoothly. Related to that is input lag, the delay between your hand and the picture. High processing lag makes you compensate with faster, tenser eye and head movements, and that fatigue is real even though you don't consciously notice it. Check whether your projector has a game or high-performance mode, since those bypass some of the image processing and often add a smoother motion setting.

The second factor is flicker from the light source. Many LED and laser projectors control brightness with pulse width modulation, turning the light on and off very rapidly, and at low brightness settings the off periods get longer. Some people are genuinely sensitive to this even when it's imperceptible, and a DLP projector's color sequencing can add what people call the rainbow effect. If your strain started right after lowering the projector's brightness, that is a strong clue; raise brightness instead of dimming, and check whether the model advertises flicker-free operation.

The third factor is brightness mismatch with the room, and it's the most common one. A large, bright projected image in a pitch-dark room is harsh, and the reverse problem also occurs: a projector too dim for a daytime room forces you to squint and lean forward. Aim for a clear image with some ambient light so you are not staring at the brightest thing in the space. Beyond that, cheap or badly set up projectors add a lot of small strain: soft focus, slight chromatic aberration at the edges of a big image, low contrast, heavy digital keystone correction, and fan noise. None is dramatic alone, but stacked together they make viewing tiring. Also consider whether your viewing distance suits the image size. A very large image from a short distance in a small studio apartment means your eyes and head are scanning far more than they would on a monitor, which is a real and often overlooked cause. Sitting farther back is a better fix than shrinking the image.

For a systematic pass on this one, change one thing per session and keep notes. Turn on game mode, then test. Set the refresh rate and resolution the projector actually supports and confirm your laptop is outputting that mode rather than a mismatched one, since odd resolutions get scaled and look mushy. Adjust brightness to match the room with a lamp on. Move back a foot or two. Add bias light behind the screen. Dim the room's overhead lights rather than the projector. Clean the lens and reposition the projector so you need little or no digital correction. If you want to test flicker specifically, point a phone camera at the screen or a white wall and look for banding, and try brightness levels to see whether the strain tracks with one setting. If none of it helps, the remaining variable is you, and the practical move is a routine eye exam, because uncorrected vision or dry eye is a far more likely cause of headaches and strain than any display setting. One thing worth knowing: according to the American Academy of Ophthalmology, ordinary screen blue light has not been shown to cause permanent eye damage, and digital eye strain is generally temporary, so blue-light glasses are not the fix; brightness, distance, room light, session length and blink rate are. The last one matters too, since focused staring cuts your blink rate substantially, and dry eyes feel exactly like screen strain.

exchanges.final_answer:
Two separate problems, and both have pretty well understood causes. Let me take them in turn.

The choppy audio is almost certainly a radio problem. Bluetooth lives in the 2.4 gigahertz band, and so does most Wi-Fi, so when your laptop is pulling real traffic over 2.4 gigahertz while simultaneously streaming audio to the JBL, the two are sharing one crowded lane. Bluetooth tries to dodge Wi-Fi with adaptive frequency hopping, jumping among its channels hundreds of times a second, but when a Wi-Fi channel is wide or the band is congested, it runs out of clean slots and packets get dropped, which is exactly the stutter you hear. This is worse on laptops because the Wi-Fi and Bluetooth radios are usually on the same little chip and share an antenna, so they have to negotiate for airtime internally. That is why the symptom appears "when I connect my laptop" but not when something else is the source.

The other candidates worth knowing: unshielded USB 3.0 devices radiate broadband noise right into the 2.4 to 2.5 gigahertz range, so a plugged-in external drive, dock, or HDMI-to-USB adapter can act like a local jammer. Windows power management can briefly power down the Bluetooth adapter to save energy. And if the audio codec is a high-bitrate one, or the laptop is under heavy CPU load while gaming, the audio buffer can underrun and sound choppy even with a clean radio link.

Here is how I would narrow it down, one variable at a time. First, switch the laptop to a 5 or 6 gigahertz Wi-Fi network and test the same local audio. If the stutter vanishes on 5 gigahertz and returns on 2.4, you have your answer, and the fix is to keep the laptop off 2.4 gigahertz, or at least move the router to a channel farther from the edges of the band. Verify the live connection rather than assuming; on Windows, netsh wlan show interfaces tells you the band and channel you are actually on, and a laptop that supports 5 gigahertz will still quietly connect to 2.4. Second, if it stutters on every band, unplug any USB 3.0 drive, hub, or dock and see whether it clears; if it does, move that device to a USB 2.0 port or put a short shielded extension cable between it and the laptop. Third, in Device Manager, open the Bluetooth adapter's properties and turn off "allow the computer to turn off this device to save power." Fourth, update the Wi-Fi and Bluetooth drivers from the laptop manufacturer, since coexistence handling is driver-dependent and generic tweaks you read online may not exist for your chipset. Fifth, move the JBL closer to the laptop with a clear line of sight, keep it off a metal desk surface, and make sure the projector isn't also holding a Bluetooth connection or a second audio profile, since each extra link eats bandwidth. If the projector is receiving the laptop's video wirelessly over Miracast, AirPlay or a casting dongle, that is another heavy 2.4 gigahertz consumer, and switching it to 5 gigahertz or using a plain HDMI cable instead is often the single biggest improvement.

Now the eye strain, which is a different kind of problem and also fairly predictable. The biggest factor is refresh rate and motion handling. A typical projector runs at 60 hertz, while a gaming monitor is often 120 to 144 hertz or more, so fast motion on the projector has more strobing and blur, and your eyes keep trying to track targets that the display isn't actually rendering smoothly. Related to that is input lag, the delay between your hand and the picture. High processing lag makes you compensate with faster, tenser eye and head movements, and that fatigue is real even though you don't consciously notice it. Check whether your projector has a game or high-performance mode, since those bypass some of the image processing and often add a smoother motion setting.

The second factor is flicker from the light source. Many LED and laser projectors control brightness with pulse width modulation, turning the light on and off very rapidly, and at low brightness settings the off periods get longer. Some people are genuinely sensitive to this even when it's imperceptible, and a DLP projector's color sequencing can add what people call the rainbow effect. If your strain started right after lowering the projector's brightness, that is a strong clue; raise brightness instead of dimming, and check whether the model advertises flicker-free operation.

The third factor is brightness mismatch with the room, and it's the most common one. A large, bright projected image in a pitch-dark room is harsh, and the reverse problem also occurs: a projector too dim for a daytime room forces you to squint and lean forward. Aim for a clear image with some ambient light so you are not staring at the brightest thing in the space. Beyond that, cheap or badly set up projectors add a lot of small strain: soft focus, slight chromatic aberration at the edges of a big image, low contrast, heavy digital keystone correction, and fan noise. None is dramatic alone, but stacked together they make viewing tiring. Also consider whether your viewing distance suits the image size. A very large image from a short distance in a small studio apartment means your eyes and head are scanning far more than they would on a monitor, which is a real and often overlooked cause. Sitting farther back is a better fix than shrinking the image.

For a systematic pass on this one, change one thing per session and keep notes. Turn on game mode, then test. Set the refresh rate and resolution the projector actually supports and confirm your laptop is outputting that mode rather than a mismatched one, since odd resolutions get scaled and look mushy. Adjust brightness to match the room with a lamp on. Move back a foot or two. Add bias light behind the screen. Dim the room's overhead lights rather than the projector. Clean the lens and reposition the projector so you need little or no digital correction. If you want to test flicker specifically, point a phone camera at the screen or a white wall and look for banding, and try brightness levels to see whether the strain tracks with one setting. If none of it helps, the remaining variable is you, and the practical move is a routine eye exam, because uncorrected vision or dry eye is a far more likely cause of headaches and strain than any display setting. One thing worth knowing: according to the American Academy of Ophthalmology, ordinary screen blue light has not been shown to cause permanent eye damage, and digital eye strain is generally temporary, so blue-light glasses are not the fix; brightness, distance, room light, session length and blink rate are. The last one matters too, since focused staring cuts your blink rate substantially, and dry eyes feel exactly like screen strain.

If you tell me the projector model, how the laptop is connected to it, and whether the laptop is on 2.4 or 5 gigahertz, I can turn this into a much shorter list of the two or three things most likely to fix it.

Here's what stands out from the past month, roughly October 13 through today, November 12.

First, Mistral finally made good on its promise. It previewed Mistral Large 4, nicknamed "Le Chonk," through its API on October 6, then published the weights on Hugging Face on October 29. It's a natively multimodal mixture of experts with about 1.05 trillion total parameters and roughly 52 billion active per token, a million token context, and a 1.6 billion parameter vision encoder. Mistral leans hardest on coding and cyber defense here, reporting 51 percent on the Artificial Analysis Cyber Index and 97.1 percent attack resistance on its own B3 security benchmark, up from 93.3 in preview. Those are vendor numbers. The weights come under what Mistral calls its Ecosystem Open-Weight license, a modified MIT that allows commercial use and fine tuning but requires a separate deal to offer the model as a hosted service. Hosting it yourself is not a hobby: sources describe an eight-GPU Blackwell node or two H100-class 80GB nodes, with specialized vLLM and SGLang images.

Second, Meta changed shape entirely. There is no Llama 5; its 2026 models ship under the Muse name, and for most of the year the frontier ones were closed. On October 15, Meta Superintelligence Labs released Muse Spark Open, 816 billion parameters with about 42 billion active, natively multimodal with text, image, video and audio input, and a million token context. Meta calls it the most capable US open-weights model to date; Artificial Analysis scored it 39 on its Intelligence Index, well above the median of about 19 for similar-size open models, but behind GLM 5.3 at 45 and Kimi K3 at 44. The catch is the license and the hardware. The Muse Model License requires a "Built with Muse Spark Open" notice in your product, and model-as-a-service companies over $20 million in revenue need a separate agreement. Meta and Apple demonstrated local inference on two Mac Studios with 512GB of unified memory each, so this is open weights in name more than something a developer can actually run.

Third, DeepSeek opened up its plumbing, not just its models. On October 17 it posted DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash-1017 to Hugging Face under a plain MIT license, a modest update that raises its agentic and coding numbers, notably 77.0 on DeepSWE on DeepSeek's own table. Three days later it released DeepInfer, the inference framework that actually serves its API, free under Apache 2.0, which Gizmodo and Bloomberg framed as pressure on OpenAI and Anthropic. Then on October 31 it put the open-source prototype of its Super-Agent on GitHub, which Bloomberg reported on November 1 as aimed squarely at Claude Code. Artificial Analysis said the Flash model was the strongest publicly available model on its Cyber Index at 57 percent, second overall only to a restricted-access OpenAI model. Independent rankings also credit V4.1 Flash with leading among models under a genuinely permissive MIT license.

Fourth, Moonshot quietly produced what several rankings now call the best open-weights model in the world. Kimi K3.1 Pro launched as an API on October 23 at $2 per million input and $10 per million output tokens, with a 2.8 trillion parameter-class mixture of experts and a million token context, and it published the weights a couple of days ago, either November 2 or 4 depending on the source, on schedule. Artificial Analysis placed it fourth overall on its Intelligence Index at 55, behind only two Claude models, and that narrowed the open-versus-closed gap from roughly 12 points to about 3. One caution: its license is Moonshot's own and carries commercial restrictions, and Artificial Analysis flagged a big gap between Moonshot's claimed 8.3 percent hallucination rate and the 44 percent it measured.

Fifth, the two Chinese giants moved in opposite directions. Alibaba opened Qwen4-Max in preview on November 11, its first Qwen4 model, with a million token context and image and video input, but only through a paid Token Plan subscription, with no weights, no model card, no benchmarks, no price, and a hard retirement date of November 25. Slides at Alibaba's conferences named Max, Plus, Flash and a 27B tier, and a 27B open-weight model is what people are waiting for, but as of today nothing is published and no date is given. Tencent, by contrast, released Hy4 on November 4, a 770 billion parameter mixture of experts with a million token context that adds native visual reasoning and computer use, meaning it can drive browsers and desktop software, and Tencent says the weights and a system card are coming shortly, so I'd treat the open-weight part as promised rather than done.

Mistral is the one selling scale and sovereignty, a trillion-parameter European-trained model under a usable-but-not-free license, positioned on cybersecurity. Meta has the biggest and most capable-looking US open-weight release, but its custom license and the 512GB-class hardware needs make it more of a showcase than a daily driver. Only eleven or thirteen games have been played, so anything I give you is a hot-start ranking, not a settled one. That said, here's how I'd order the top five as of tonight, based on the numbers that multiple stat sites agree on.

First, Victor Wembanyama. Through twelve games he's at about thirty points, eleven and a half rebounds and four and a quarter blocks a game, shooting over fifty-four percent from the field, and his team is on a nine-game win streak. What separates him from everyone else is the two-way part: he's a top-two scorer while leading the league in blocks, and on HoopsHype's Global Rating, which blends individual production with team impact and penalizes missed games, he scores thirty-five point oh five against thirty point four eight for the next man. He did forty points, eleven rebounds and eight blocks in twenty-five minutes at Phoenix, and fifty-two points and twenty-four rebounds against Dallas. Advanced defensive value is hard to see in a box score, but a shot-blocker of his caliber changes what opponents attempt, and the Spurs' win streak is the visible version of that.

Second, Luka Dončić, who is having arguably the greatest scoring start ever: thirty-eight and a half to thirty-nine points a game with about seven and a half rebounds, seven and a half assists and two steals, at roughly sixty-five to sixty-seven percent true shooting. That's absurd efficiency at a huge volume. The Lakers are ten and two, and nine and two in the eleven games he played, with an average plus-minus around plus fifteen according to one game-log site. He ranks second on everything I looked at, and the only reason he's behind Wembanyama for me is defense: Dončić's impact is almost entirely offensive, while Wembanyama changes games at both ends.

Third, Nikola Jokić, and this one is closer than the numbers look. Twenty-three and a half points, ten and a half rebounds and nine assists, but his true shooting has dropped to about fifty-seven percent from sixty-seven last year, and he's coming off an elbow sprain. Denver isn't as good as it was. Still, he leads all centers by a wide margin in playmaking, and his Global Rating of twenty-six is comfortably ahead of everyone below him, because his team's offense is essentially his passing.

Fourth, Giannis Antetokounmpo, who has made the transition to Miami look easy: twenty-seven and a half points, twelve and a half rebounds, five assists, and fifty-nine percent shooting. His free-throw shooting, around sixty-two percent, is the one real blemish on his efficiency. I'd put him above the fifth spot because of rebounds and rim pressure, though his blocks have fallen to about one a game, which suggests Miami isn't leaning on him defensively the way Milwaukee did.

Fifth, Shai Gilgeous-Alexander, the back-to-back MVP, at about twenty-nine and a half points a game. He's still the most reliable late-game scorer in the league, but by this season's current impact metrics he's ninth in the HoopsHype rating and his supporting numbers, four and a half assists and low rebounding, don't separate him from good guards. Nobody outside Wembanyama, Dončić and Jokić has as high a floor, but right now he's the weakest claim to this top five of the five I picked.

Right behind them, in roughly this order: Jamal Murray, Tyrese Maxey, Jayson Tatum, Cooper Flagg, Deni Avdija and Jalen Brunson, with Brunson a real candidate if you weight the Knicks' start and his Player of the Week more heavily than I did.

Two honest caveats. Different sites disagree slightly on these averages depending on which games they've counted, so Luka at thirty-eight point six on one site is thirty-nine point three on another. And I couldn't pull reliable playing-plus-minus or box plus-minus values for this season from the sources I reached, so the advanced part of this ranking leans mostly on HoopsHype's Global Rating and on true shooting percentages, which I do consider the fairest single efficiency measure.

The Spurs extinguished the Suns for their ninth win in a row, a 122-96 blowout behind another masterful performance from Victor Wembanyama.
Here's every way Wembanyama dominated the Suns:
## Defensive Menace
Wembanyama almost logged a triple-double with blocks, and blocked two shots on a single possession two separate times in this game. He talked his talk, pumping his fist after returning one to sender and then turning his palms up at his opponent with a furrowed brow as if to say, "why'd you try to do that?'
## Shot Selection, Balanced Aggression
"We're playing the right way, we're playing with and for each other, this is the basketball I like," Wembanyama said.
## Transition Rim Running
This Spurs team is unbelievably dangerous in transition, and when Wembanyama gets behind the defense it's about as easy as two points can be.
In the first quarter, Steph Castle dropped it off to a hard-charging Wembanyama who caught the ball at the elbow, deftly took his two steps through the defense, and dunked with two hands for safety.
## A Very Foxy Pick and Roll
Wembanyama leads the NBA with 36 alley-oops this year including four on Monday night. De'Aaron Fox and Stephon Castle serve up the vast majority of those lobs, and recently the Spurs are dialing in that pick and roll with Fox to inflict maximum punishment.
When Wembanyama sets a screen and Fox dribbles to his dominant left hand with speed, the defense is more compromised than a honeypotted tech CEO.
## Heads-up Passing
Wembanyama draws so much attention that the give-and-go should work wonders, and Steph Castle sort of stumbled into one for a highlight play. He bailed out of a corner 3 when the defender closed out well, getting the ball to Wembanyama a few feet away. When the ball went to Wemby so did the eyes and bodies of the three nearest defenders, leaving Castle a wide open lane to the hoop. Wembanyama bounced the ball back just as soon as he caught it, and Steph slammed a tomahawk down.

Only eleven or thirteen games have been played, so anything I give you is a hot-start ranking, not a settled one. That said, here's how I'd order the top five as of tonight, based on the numbers that multiple stat sites agree on.

First, Victor Wembanyama. Through twelve games he's at about thirty points, eleven and a half rebounds and four and a quarter blocks a game, shooting over fifty-four percent from the field, and his team is on a nine-game win streak. What separates him from everyone else is the two-way part: he's a top-two scorer while leading the league in blocks, and on HoopsHype's Global Rating, which blends individual production with team impact and penalizes missed games, he scores thirty-five point oh five against thirty point four eight for the next man. He did forty points, eleven rebounds and eight blocks in twenty-five minutes at Phoenix, and fifty-two points and twenty-four rebounds against Dallas. Advanced defensive value is hard to see in a box score, but a shot-blocker of his caliber changes what opponents attempt, and the Spurs' win streak is the visible version of that.

Second, Luka Dončić, who is having arguably the greatest scoring start ever: thirty-eight and a half to thirty-nine points a game with about seven and a half rebounds, seven and a half assists and two steals, at roughly sixty-five to sixty-seven percent true shooting. That's absurd efficiency at a huge volume. The Lakers are ten and two, and nine and two in the eleven games he played, with an average plus-minus around plus fifteen according to one game-log site. He ranks second on everything I looked at, and the only reason he's behind Wembanyama for me is defense: Dončić's impact is almost entirely offensive, while Wembanyama changes games at both ends.

Third, Nikola Jokić, and this one is closer than the numbers look. Twenty-three and a half points, ten and a half rebounds and nine assists, but his true shooting has dropped to about fifty-seven percent from sixty-seven last year, and he's coming off an elbow sprain. Denver isn't as good as it was. Still, he leads all centers by a wide margin in playmaking, and his Global Rating of twenty-six is comfortably ahead of everyone below him, because his team's offense is essentially his passing.

Fourth, Giannis Antetokounmpo, who has made the transition to Miami look easy: twenty-seven and a half points, twelve and a half rebounds, five assists, and fifty-nine percent shooting. His free-throw shooting, around sixty-two percent, is the one real blemish on his efficiency. I'd put him above the fifth spot because of rebounds and rim pressure, though his blocks have fallen to about one a game, which suggests Miami isn't leaning on him defensively the way Milwaukee did.

Fifth, Shai Gilgeous-Alexander, the back-to-back MVP, at about twenty-nine and a half points a game. He's still the most reliable late-game scorer in the league, but by this season's current impact metrics he's ninth in the HoopsHype rating and his supporting numbers, four and a half assists and low rebounding, don't separate him from good guards. Nobody outside Wembanyama, Dončić and Jokić has as high a floor, but right now he's the weakest claim to this top five of the five I picked.

Right behind them, in roughly this order: Jamal Murray, Tyrese Maxey, Jayson Tatum, Cooper Flagg, Deni Avdija and Jalen Brunson, with Brunson a real candidate if you weight the Knicks' start and his Player of the Week more heavily than I did.

Two honest caveats. Different sites disagree slightly on these averages depending on which games they've counted, so Luka at thirty-eight point six on one site is thirty-nine point three on another. And I couldn't pull reliable playing-plus-minus or box plus-minus values for this season from the sources I reached, so the advanced part of this ranking leans mostly on HoopsHype's Global Rating and on true shooting percentages, which I do consider the fairest single efficiency measure.

Here's what I found for November 12, 2026. Rates on savings are variable, so these are today's posted numbers, and the interest figures assume the rate holds for a full year, which is optimistic.

Starting with the five that actually qualify as high-yield.

Marcus by Goldman Sachs is the highest of the well-known names at 3.50% APY. On 50,000 dollars that's about 1,750 dollars in a year. No minimum to open, no minimum balance to earn the rate, no monthly fee. It's savings-only, so no debit card on the account.

Ally Bank is at 3.20% APY, which works out to about 1,600 dollars. No minimum to open or to keep, no monthly fee.

Capital One's 360 Performance Savings is also 3.20% APY, about 1,600 dollars. Flat rate on all balances, no minimum balance, no monthly fee. Worth noting Capital One sells a separate, lower-rate product called plain 360 Savings, so make sure you're getting the Performance Savings one.

American Express High Yield Savings is 3.20% APY, about 1,600 dollars. No minimum to open, no minimum balance for the rate, no fee. It does allow nine transactions a month instead of the usual six.

CIT Bank Platinum Savings pays 3.75% APY, about 1,875 dollars, but that rate only applies to balances of 5,000 dollars or more, so your 50,000 clears it easily. Below 5,000 the rate drops to 0.25%. There's also a promotion running through December 15 that adds 0.60 percentage points for six months for new customers, which would push the first half-year above 4% before reverting. Minimum to open is 100 dollars.

So the high-yield group clusters tightly: 1,600 to 1,875 dollars on your 50,000. The gap between the best and worst of those five is only about 275 dollars a year.

Now the contrast, because it matters. Chase's standard savings account is paying 0.01% APY, which is about 5 dollars a year on your money. Bank of America is 0.04%, about 20 dollars. Wells Fargo, Truist and U.S. Bank's standard rates are in the same range, 0.01% to 0.05%. That's why switching is worth doing. Moving 50,000 from Chase to Marcus is roughly 1,745 dollars a year of difference.

One trap worth flagging: U.S. Bank advertises 2.00% APY, but only on balances between 5,000 and just under 25,000 dollars, and only with a linked Bank Smartly Checking account. Your 50,000 wouldn't fit that tier, so the advertised number wouldn't apply.

Two caveats. Every rate I quoted is variable and these accounts move with Fed policy. The Fed held rates steady in October, and the remaining late-2026 meeting isn't expected to cut, but a cut in 2027 would pull these down. Also, the FDIC national average for savings is 0.38% as of October, so all five of these are well above average, and all five are FDIC-insured, though 50,000 is comfortably under the 250,000 coverage limit at any single bank.

I'd treat the exact APYs as today's snapshot and confirm each one on the bank's own site before moving money.

Here's what I found for November 12, 2026. Rates on savings are variable, so these are today's posted numbers, and the interest figures assume the rate holds for a full year, which is optimistic.

Starting with the five that actually qualify as high-yield.

Marcus by Goldman Sachs is the highest of the well-known names at 3.50% APY. On 50,000 dollars that's about 1,750 dollars in a year. No minimum to open, no minimum balance to earn the rate, no monthly fee. It's savings-only, so no debit card on the account.

Ally Bank is at 3.20% APY, which works out to about 1,600 dollars. No minimum to open or to keep, no monthly fee.

Capital One's 360 Performance Savings is also 3.20% APY, about 1,600 dollars. Flat rate on all balances, no minimum balance, no monthly fee. Worth noting Capital One sells a separate, lower-rate product called plain 360 Savings, so make sure you're getting the Performance Savings one.

American Express High Yield Savings is 3.20% APY, about 1,600 dollars. No minimum to open, no minimum balance for the rate, no fee. It does allow nine transactions a month instead of the usual six.

CIT Bank Platinum Savings pays 3.75% APY, about 1,875 dollars, but that rate only applies to balances of 5,000 dollars or more, so your 50,000 clears it easily. Below 5,000 the rate drops to 0.25%. There's also a promotion running through December 15 that adds 0.60 percentage points for six months for new customers, which would push the first half-year above 4% before reverting. Minimum to open is 100 dollars.

So the high-yield group clusters tightly: 1,600 to 1,875 dollars on your 50,000. The gap between the best and worst of those five is only about 275 dollars a year.

Now the contrast, because it matters. Chase's standard savings account is paying 0.01% APY, which is about 5 dollars a year on your money. Bank of America is 0.04%, about 20 dollars. Wells Fargo, Truist and U.S. Bank's standard rates are in the same range, 0.01% to 0.05%. That's why switching is worth doing. Moving 50,000 from Chase to Marcus is roughly 1,745 dollars a year of difference.

One trap worth flagging: U.S. Bank advertises 2.00% APY, but only on balances between 5,000 and just under 25,000 dollars, and only with a linked Bank Smartly Checking account. Your 50,000 wouldn't fit that tier, so the advertised number wouldn't apply.

Hupo, from the Michelin Guide: Bib Gourmand | $$ | Chinese | Queens | 1007 50th Ave., Queens
The inspector says: Sometimes you can hear the sound of sizzling woks drifting from the kitchen at this Long Island City spot. The sleek, narrow dining room is comfortable and understated, setting the tone for a focused menu that favors clarity over excess. Expect approachable takes on regional favorites, like lightly dressed cucumber batons scented with sesame and peppercorn, ma-la wontons awash in a sweet-spicy sauce, and mapo tofu built around large, fresh cubes of house-made tofu with leeks and scallions. Heat is present but restrained, emphasizing aroma and balance rather than sheer intensity. Hupo may not court thrill-seekers, but it offers a gentle, repeatable expression of Sichuan cooking that works especially well for everyday dining.

The inspector says: Hiding behind a banchan shop in Long Island City, this intimate chef’s counter is as much a classroom as it is a restaurant. Chef Hooni Kim builds a deeply personal menu around Korean fermentation, drawing on kimchi, doenjang, gochujang, ganjang, ssamjang, and other products that have been aged for years. His philosophy extends beyond flavor to ideas of nourishment, tradition, and the relationship between food and digestion, all of which he shares freely with guests. These fermented ingredients lend remarkable depth to deceptively simple dishes, from silky tofu with doenjang to beef with ssamjang. Later, a comforting spread of rice, pork, fried egg, seaweed, and deeply flavored aged kimchi brings the experience closest to Korean home cooking.

Here are five places clustered around 49th and 50th Avenues in Long Island City, all within a few blocks of one another, so they're genuinely walkable from anywhere in the neighborhood. I'd caveat that I'm assuming you're somewhere in central LIC near the QueensMidtown area; if you're out near the waterfront or the eastern edge, add ten minutes or so.

**Casa Enrique**, 5-48 49th Avenue. Mexican, from Chiapas, run by chef Cosme Aguilar. It was a Michelin one-star winner for years and is still listed in the guide at the moderate two-dollar-sign level, so call it thirty to fifty a person with drinks. It's rated 4.4 out of 5 on Tripadvisor and ranked number three of 176 restaurants in LIC. The reason to go is the mole, excellent in every form, plus bigger plates like branzino al pastor and a braised lamb shank in a fruity-spicy broth. There's almost always a crowd out front, so a reservation helps.

**Meju**, 5-28 49th Avenue, hiding in the back of the Little Banchan Shop. This is the ambitious one: one Michelin star, Korean, an eight-seat chef's counter where Hooni Kim builds everything around his own fermented pastes, kimchi, doenjang, gochujang, aged for years. It's a tasting menu at about two hundred thirty-five a person on the restaurant's own site, though a couple of review sites still quote two hundred fifteen, so budget two to three hundred with wine. Reservations are released at nine in the morning and they go fast, and it only runs a few nights a week. Worth it if you want a three-hour, quietly educational meal rather than dinner with friends talking over it.

**Hupo**, 10-07 50th Avenue. Sichuan Chinese, Michelin Bib Gourmand, meaning good value for the money, listed at two dollar signs. Expect somewhere in the forties per person. Michelin's inspector likes it for everyday dining, saying the heat is present but restrained, favoring aroma and balance, with house-made tofu in mapo and ma-la wontons. One note of caution on price: The Infatuation tags it at four dollar signs, so if you order several mains and a good bottle it can creep up. Its Tripadvisor review count is very small, so I'd trust the Michelin and Yelp signal more than a single aggregate score here.

**Vert Frais**, 43-10 Crescent Street. Japanese, listed in the guide without a star and in Michelin's best-ramen-in-NYC roundup, two dollar signs, so twenty-five to fifty. It's a bright white-walled café with communal tables, backed by Nobuyuki Shikanai of Kanoyama. Go for the shio ramen with cleanly charred cha-shu, a pork or salmon rice bowl, and the tall jiggly soufflé pancakes. It's the casual one of the five, good for brunch or a solo lunch, not a destination dinner.

**R40**, 47-16 Vernon Boulevard, right on the waterfront side. Argentinian, three dollar signs, so seventy to a hundred and ten a person depending how much meat you order. This is a wood-fired parilla, big cuts over an open grill, the smoke drifting through a long room of wood and exposed brick, with a greenhouse-y back patio. Empanadas stuffed with filet mignon and raisins, skirt steak with chimichurri, and a combination platter of steak, ribs, chorizo and sweetbreads that Michelin warns is only for serious appetites. The Infatuation pegs it as a date-night spot and mentions a tasting menu around a hundred five. Again, its Tripadvisor count is thin, so treat the guide and The Infatuation as the better read.

One honest limitation: outside Casa Enrique, I couldn't pin down a solid single numeric rating for these. Several are newer and barely reviewed on Tripadvisor, so their Michelin status and the critics I found are the more reliable evidence of quality. exchanges.final_answer:
Here are five places clustered around 49th and 50th Avenues in Long Island City, all within a few blocks of one another, so they're genuinely walkable from anywhere in the neighborhood. I'd caveat that I'm assuming you're somewhere in central LIC near the QueensMidtown area; if you're out near the waterfront or the eastern edge, add ten minutes or so.

**Casa Enrique**, 5-48 49th Avenue. Mexican, from Chiapas, run by chef Cosme Aguilar. It was a Michelin one-star winner for years and is still listed in the guide at the moderate two-dollar-sign level, so call it thirty to fifty a person with drinks. It's rated 4.4 out of 5 on Tripadvisor and ranked number three of 176 restaurants in LIC. The reason to go is the mole, excellent in every form, plus bigger plates like branzino al pastor and a braised lamb shank in a fruity-spicy broth. There's almost always a crowd out front, so a reservation helps.

**Meju**, 5-28 49th Avenue, hiding in the back of the Little Banchan Shop. This is the ambitious one: one Michelin star, Korean, an eight-seat chef's counter where Hooni Kim builds everything around his own fermented pastes, kimchi, doenjang, gochujang, aged for years. It's a tasting menu at about two hundred thirty-five a person on the restaurant's own site, though a couple of review sites still quote two hundred fifteen, so budget two to three hundred with wine. Reservations are released at nine in the morning and they go fast, and it only runs a few nights a week. Worth it if you want a three-hour, quietly educational meal rather than dinner with friends talking over it.

**Hupo**, 10-07 50th Avenue. Sichuan Chinese, Michelin Bib Gourmand, meaning good value for the money, listed at two dollar signs. Expect somewhere in the forties per person. Michelin's inspector likes it for everyday dining, saying the heat is present but restrained, favoring aroma and balance, with house-made tofu in mapo and ma-la wontons. One note of caution on price: The Infatuation tags it at four dollar signs, so if you order several mains and a good bottle it can creep up. Its Tripadvisor review count is very small, so I'd trust the Michelin and Yelp signal more than a single aggregate score here.

**Vert Frais**, 43-10 Crescent Street. Japanese, listed in the guide without a star and in Michelin's best-ramen-in-NYC roundup, two dollar signs, so twenty-five to fifty. It's a bright white-walled café with communal tables, backed by Nobuyuki Shikanai of Kanoyama. Go for the shio ramen with cleanly charred cha-shu, a pork or salmon rice bowl, and the tall jiggly soufflé pancakes. It's the casual one of the five, good for brunch or a solo lunch, not a destination dinner.

**R40**, 47-16 Vernon Boulevard, right on the waterfront side. Argentinian, three dollar signs, so seventy to a hundred and ten a person depending how much meat you order. This is a wood-fired parilla, big cuts over an open grill, the smoke drifting through a long room of wood and exposed brick, with a greenhouse-y back patio. Empanadas stuffed with filet mignon and raisins, skirt steak with chimichurri, and a combination platter of steak, ribs, chorizo and sweetbreads that Michelin warns is only for serious appetites. The Infatuation pegs it as a date-night spot and mentions a tasting menu around a hundred five. Again, its Tripadvisor count is thin, so treat the guide and The Infatuation as the better read.

One honest limitation: outside Casa Enrique, I couldn't pin down a solid single numeric rating for these. Several are newer and barely reviewed on Tripadvisor, so their Michelin status and the critics I found are the more reliable evidence of quality. If you tell me which night and how many people, I can help you sequence the cheap ones against Meju, since booking that counter is the hard part.

The standard pass runs on consecutive days: an 8-day pass covers 8 days in a row. The Swiss Travel Pass Flex (from CHF 289) gives you the same number of travel days to use on any dates within one month — you activate each day before your first ride.

Second class is comfortable, clean and how most Swiss travel — it is the right default. Quick correction first: the Fed didn't cut to zero last month. As of now the federal funds target range is 3.75 to 4 percent, and the last actual move was the opposite of a cut — a quarter-point *increase* that took effect September 17, 2026. The October 28 meeting held rates there, and the Fed's own September projections had the median official seeing rates around 4.1 percent by the end of this year, with markets leaning toward another hike at the December 8-to-9 meeting rather than a cut.

That matters for your question, because mortgage rates don't follow the fed funds rate very closely anyway; they track the ten-year Treasury and mortgage-backed securities. And those have been firm. Right now averages are roughly 7.0 to 7.2 percent on a 30-year fixed purchase loan, with refinance offers a bit higher, around 7.4 percent, and the 15-year around 6.5 percent. Freddie Mac's weekly survey had 30-year at 7.18 on November 6, down a little from an October high of about 7.40 but well above February's low near 6. So the rate environment is not the sort that rewards waiting, and it certainly isn't a zero-rate environment.

So the honest answer is: it depends entirely on what rate you're paying now, and a Fed headline isn't the reason to do it. The rule of thumb is that refinancing is worth a hard look if you can cut your rate by roughly three-quarters of a percentage point or more and you plan to stay in the home long enough for the monthly savings to repay the closing costs, which usually run somewhere around 2 to 5 percent of the loan balance. If you're sitting on an old loan at 3 or 4 percent, refinancing at today's rates would almost certainly cost you money. If you're at 7.5 or 8 percent, or you have an adjustable rate that's about to reset, or mortgage insurance you could drop, it may well be worth it.
